selected_pair.title: Why Did Higher Wages Buy Less?
selected_pair.reason: The script’s central reversal is that nominal pay rises while modeled basket affordability worsens; this pair expresses that mechanism immediately and promises only the comparison actually made.

concepts.title: How Many Days of Work Bought the Basics?
concepts.audience_surface: English-language history/economics viewers on long-form YouTube browse and suggested surfaces; phone-size first, with desktop preview as secondary.
concepts.promise: Make a year of necessities tangible against a finite amount of paid work.
concepts.genre_mood: Illustrated economic history; tactile, curious, grounded.
concepts.first_confirmation: The narration opens with bread, fuel and light, then states the modeled family basket and 333 wage-days versus an assumed 250.
concepts.separate_payoff: The climax shows that later silver wages more than double while the price index grows nearly threefold; the resolution reaches about 116 modeled wage-days in 1850–1899.
concepts.likely_misread: Could imply the 333 is observed days actually worked or the literal price of bread; text/title and description specify a model-implied equivalent.
concepts.hook_and_technique: Intro object/action hook; tactile necessity object plus visibly incomplete count. Transfer principle from Paper Detour 030 accepted long cover set: large concrete object and one strong contrast, rebuilt for this episode. format_id: no catalog ID available in the accessible source materials; not claimed as a measured winner.

concepts.title: When a Year’s Wages Couldn’t Cover the Basics
concepts.audience_surface: English-language history/economics viewers on phone-size YouTube browse/suggested cards.
concepts.promise: Ask whether a modeled year of wages can cover a reconstructed basic-needs basket.
concepts.genre_mood: Illustrated social/economic history; tense, empathetic, restrained.
concepts.first_confirmation: The opening explains that modeled earnings cover about three quarters of the basket, and 333 modeled wage-days exceed the assumed 250 paid days.
concepts.separate_payoff: Later periods show the basket moving above and below the basic-needs comparison, ending much lower relative to daily pay in 1850–1899.
concepts.likely_misread: Could turn a conditional model into a claim about an actual named worker or universal household; no named individual is depicted and the title says “a year’s wages.”
concepts.hook_and_technique: Material gap/absence: missing wall section makes shortfall legible without an invented historical event. Transfer principle from the accepted episode 037 cover concept “WHAT COMES FIRST?”: a visual choice among necessities; here the choice is transformed into a gap. Episode-specific figure/phrase is not copied. format_id: none available in accessible source materials.

concepts.title: Why Did Higher Wages Buy Less?
concepts.audience_surface: English-language history/economics viewers on phone-size YouTube browse/suggested cards; test title and image together.
concepts.promise: Explain how higher nominal wages could coincide with a less affordable basic basket.
concepts.genre_mood: Illustrated economic-history investigation; surprising, analytical, clear.
concepts.first_confirmation: The investigation introduces 176 wage-days for 1500–1549, then asks viewers to predict whether a later basket costs fewer or more wage-days.
concepts.separate_payoff: The climax answers “More”: about 216 days in 1600–1649, explaining that prices rose faster; the nineteenth-century comparison later falls to about 116.
concepts.likely_misread: Could suggest prices rose in modern terms or all goods rose uniformly; title and description bound claim to the script’s selected London model and historical periods.
concepts.hook_and_technique: Unequal-rise contrast as a compact visual mechanism: a two-step wage stair beside a nearly three-step price stair. Transfer principle from accepted Paper Detour 030: one strong contrast and clear large-scale read; episode-specific stairs, coin and phrase are newly composed. format_id: no measured result or available catalog ID; no CTR claim.
